title: Scoping JEAP, 2024-2026
text:
This is a space to record progress in a scoping review I am working on as a way to better make sense of what kinds of research have been published in the Journal of EAP (JEAP). I am conducting this review partly because of the need to publish as an aspect of my doctoral studies. That is, a review of JEAP published articles makes sense for a doctoral student attempting to become a member of this practitioner community by contributing to the research pool. Doing so might provide direction and inspiration for my next project.
One inspiration for the project work is the article “The contexts, theoretical and methodological orientation of EAP research: Evidence from empirical articles published in the Journal of English for Academic Purposes” (Riazi et al., 2020). I noticed, however, that the focus on ‘the empirical’ and ‘evidence’ left other types of content uncounted.
Secondly, having recently completed a Reflexive Thematic Analysis project based on methods discussed in Braun & Clarke (2022), I have found myself wondering whether there is a predominance of positivist, rather than interpretive, research within published articles. And, of course, one way to find out what kind of publications are published in JEAP is to conduct my own analysis.
Finally, as a practitioner-researcher with a full-time job, doctoral studies, and the desire to be a fully engaged parent to my young child, I sometimes wonder if the barriers for entry into the conversation are structural. I question how feasible it is to produce work for publication as a sole, unfunded individual.


The review aims to investigate what kinds of work appear in JEAP, on what epistemological terms and at what cost to produce. I am interested in who is able to participate in the field’s published conversation.

What was published, and what did it claim to do?

How were items distributed across genres?
What kinds of contribution did items of each genre claim to make?

What can be said about the epistemological frameworks of published work?

How often are epistemological or methodological positions made explicit?
Where an epistemological or methodological stance is taken, which appear and how often?

What can be said about the resources engaged in producing the publications?

What resources, such as team size, funding, and specialist requirements were employed to develop the published work?
What proportion could feasibly have been produced by a sole, unfunded practitioner-researcher at a single site within one academic year?





Approaches to conducting systematic secondary research may initially appeal to the lone developing researcher for two main reasons. However, I would argue that both contain significant complications in the pursuit of publication.
Firstly, a researcher might be interested in the popularity of such approaches. As predicted in Norris & Ortega (2007) there is a growing interest in how such research methods can be applied to the field of applied linguistics (Chong & Plonsky, 2024, p. 1570). However, as Norris & Ortega (2007), warned there are still challenging questions around how effectively systematic approaches can work across different data sources, such as quantitative and qualitative data and in response to different paradigms. This challenge echoes back to arguments made by Guba & Lincoln (1982), that constructivist (naturalistic) inquiries required a different set of trustworthiness criteria to those typically applied to rationalistic or positivist research. If scoping reviews are intended to develop an argument through analysis of a broad range of sources from different paradigms, it is an obvious challenge to develop criteria for quality research. Picking up this thread for L2 writing research Riazi et al. (2023), note that quality in qualitative research should more reasonably be based on Guba and Lincoln’s (1982) framework of trustworthiness: credibility, dependability and confirmability rather than on the ‘conventional terminology’ of ‘reliability and validity’ (Riazi et al., 2023, p. 2).










Note



to draft





The project has a basic shape and Research Questions which I have drafted as answerable from the corpus. I now need to develop a codebook. In line with my questions about the value of entirely positivist approaches to research I plan to combine records that are easily countable (and thus quantitative) with records that may take some interpretation, such as assumptions underlying methodological choices.

title: About Me
text:
I’m Ben, an Associate Lecturer at UCL focusing on materials development for our CLIE Pre-sessional Course.
I am also a part-time student, which is why I started this page. I am studying at the University of St. Andrews, and through my Doctoral Studies (to become a Doctor of Professional Practice), I have set myself the ambitious goal of completing high quality research studies that are practice focused. That is, I hope to use research projects and methods to improve the quality of the pre-sessional course in terms of teaching and learning, as well as the student and teacher experience.
My main interest is in understanding how students tackle the demands of a pre-sessional research project that involves writing from sources.
